key_facts: Chronic inflammatory disease of the **pilosebaceous unit**: comedones, papules, pustules, nodules.
Affects **85–95% of adolescents**; 20–35% moderate–severe; often persists into adulthood, especially in women.
UK care follows **NICE NG198**: 12-week fixed-combination topicals ± an oral tetracycline; **never antibiotic alone**.
Refer **acne fulminans the same day**; refer scarring or distress at any severity.

sections.title: Overview
blocks: Acne vulgaris is the common form of acne: a chronic inflammatory disorder of the **pilosebaceous unit** (the hair follicle and its sebaceous gland). It produces a mixed eruption of non-inflammatory lesions (**comedones**) and inflammatory lesions (**papules, pustules, nodules**).

ul: It favours areas with the most sebaceous follicles: **face, neck, upper chest, shoulders and back**. About half of patients have truncal acne as well as facial acne.
Diagnosis is **clinical**. Comedones are the hallmark and help separate acne from rosacea and folliculitis.
It matters beyond the skin: **scarring**, persistent pigment change and real **psychological distress**, often out of proportion to how the acne looks.
Severe variants (**acne conglobata**, **acne fulminans**) are uncommon but need specialist care.

sub: Most adolescents (about **85–95%**) have acne to some degree; **20–35%** develop moderate to severe disease.
It is one of the most common skin conditions worldwide.
Usually starts around puberty and peaks in the **mid to late teens**.
It can persist into, or begin in, adult life: roughly **50% of women in their 20s** and 30–40% in their 30s have some acne.
About **a quarter of adult women** with acne had none as teenagers (adult-onset acne).
More common and often more severe in **males during adolescence**.
More common in **females in adulthood** (hormonal and PCOS-related acne).
Affects all ethnic groups. In **skin of colour**, post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation and keloid scarring are more frequent and are often the main concern.
Strongly heritable: twin studies attribute about **80%** of the variation in acne risk to genetics.

sections.title: Aetiology: causes and risk factors
blocks: Acne results from a **genetic predisposition** acted on by androgens and local factors. No single cause is found in most patients.

ul.t: **Androgens**: drive sebum production and follicular plugging.
sub: Puberty; **polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS)**; congenital adrenal hyperplasia and other hyperandrogenic states.
Acne often changes in **pregnancy**.
Corticosteroids (systemic and topical), testosterone and **anabolic steroids**, lithium, **EGFR inhibitors**, JAK inhibitors, phenytoin, halogens (iodides, bromides).
Headbands, helmets, chin straps, backpacks, sports pads, face masks.
Occlusive or comedogenic creams and make-up; **pomade acne** along the hairline from greasy hair products.

ul: **Picking and squeezing**, humid environments and heavy sweating.

ul.t: **Diet**: links with high-glycaemic foods and dairy (and whey protein supplements) have been reported, but **NICE finds insufficient evidence to recommend any specific acne diet**.
sub: A balanced diet is reasonable; strict exclusion diets are not.

ul.t: **Dirt or poor hygiene** does not cause acne.
sub: The dark colour of a blackhead is oxidised keratin and melanin, not dirt. Over-washing and scrubbing make irritation worse.

ul: **Acne is not infectious** and cannot be caught.
**Sunlight does not cure acne**: any improvement is temporary, and retinoids and tetracyclines increase sun sensitivity.

blocks.title: Drug-induced acneiform eruptions
blocks.text: A sudden, **monomorphic** papulopustular eruption without comedones after starting a drug (steroids, EGFR inhibitors) is an acneiform drug eruption rather than acne vulgaris.

sections.title: Pathophysiology and pathology
blocks: Four linked processes act in a single follicle. They explain each lesion type and which drug targets which step.

mech.t: At puberty, androgens (testosterone, DHEAS) enlarge the sebaceous glands and increase **sebum** output. IGF-1 also stimulates the glands, which may explain the reported link with high-glycaemic diets.
mech.caption: Step 1: androgens from the blood stimulate an enlarged sebaceous gland to pour excess sebum into the follicle.

mech.t: Keratinocytes lining the upper follicle multiply and fail to shed. Sticky keratin and sebum **plug the follicle**, forming a **microcomedone**, the precursor of every acne lesion. A closed plug is a whitehead; a plug open to the surface is a blackhead.
mech.caption: Step 2: sticky keratinocytes and sebum plug the follicle opening, forming a comedone.

mech.t: The plugged, lipid-rich, low-oxygen follicle lets the commensal ***C. acnes*** multiply. It activates **Toll-like receptor 2** on immune cells, releasing IL-1β, IL-8, IL-12 and TNF-α; Th17 cells and IL-17 recruit neutrophils.
mech.caption: Step 3: C. acnes multiplies inside the plug and immune cells gather around the follicle wall.

mech.t: Inflammation turns comedones into **papules and pustules**. If the follicle wall ruptures, keratin, sebum and bacteria spill into the dermis, causing a deeper **nodule** and, when healing is disordered, **scarring** or pigment change.
mech.caption: Step 4: the follicle ruptures into the dermis, producing a pustule and deeper inflammatory nodule.

fig.caption: One follicle, five stages: normal → closed comedone → open comedone → inflamed papule-pustule → deep nodule.
fig.alt: Five follicle cross-sections from normal to nodule

blocks.h: How treatments map onto the mechanism

ul: **Retinoids** (adapalene, tretinoin; isotretinoin): normalise keratinisation and unplug follicles (step 2). Isotretinoin also shrinks sebaceous glands (step 1).
**Benzoyl peroxide**: kills *C. acnes* without resistance and is mildly comedolytic (steps 2–3).
**Antibiotics** (topical clindamycin, oral tetracyclines): reduce *C. acnes* and are anti-inflammatory (steps 3–4).
**Azelaic acid**: antibacterial, comedolytic and reduces pigmentation.
**Combined pill and antiandrogens**: reduce androgen-driven sebum (step 1).

histo: **Microcomedone / comedone**: dilated follicular infundibulum filled with compact keratin and sebum; a narrow (closed) or wide (open) opening.
**Inflammatory papule / pustule**: perifollicular lymphocytes, then neutrophils; follicular wall thinning.
**Ruptured follicle / nodule**: dermal abscess with a **foreign-body granulomatous** reaction to keratin and hair.
**Scar**: dermal fibrosis (hypertrophic or keloid) or loss of dermal tissue (atrophic ice-pick, rolling, boxcar).
Biopsy is **rarely needed**; histology is mainly used when another diagnosis is suspected.

sections.title: Clinical features

ul: Often few physical symptoms; inflamed papules and nodules can be **tender or painful**.
Oily skin (**seborrhoea**) is common.
Ask about the **psychological impact**: embarrassment, social withdrawal, low mood, bullying.
Systemic symptoms (fever, joint pain) are **not** part of ordinary acne: think **acne fulminans**.

blocks: Several lesion types usually occur together. Individual lesions last under 2 weeks; deep nodules can persist for months.

lesions.name: Open comedones (blackheads)
lesions.t: Dilated follicles with a dark keratin plug at the surface. Non-inflammatory.

lesions.name: Closed comedones (whiteheads)
lesions.t: Small skin-coloured or white papules with no visible opening; easiest to see with side lighting.

lesions.name: Papules
lesions.t: Small (< 5 mm), tender, red bumps arising from inflamed comedones.

lesions.name: Pustules
lesions.t: Papules with a visible white or yellow centre of pus.

lesions.name: Nodules and pseudocysts
lesions.t: Large, deep, painful red lumps (≥ 5 mm) or fluctuant cyst-like swellings. High risk of scarring: needs oral treatment or referral.

lesions.name: Secondary lesions
lesions.t: Excoriations, red marks (**post-inflammatory erythema**), dark marks (**post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation**) and **scars**.

bodymap.caption: Where acne appears: face, central chest, upper back and shoulders. Truncal involvement shapes the choice of treatment.
pts: **Face** (most common): forehead, cheeks, nose, chin and jawline.
**Trunk**: upper chest, upper back and shoulders, in about half of patients.
Adult female acne favours the **lower face and jawline**.
Pomade acne follows the **hairline**; acne mechanica follows the area of friction.

variants.name: Comedonal acne
variants.t: Mainly open and closed comedones with few inflamed lesions. Topical retinoid territory.

variants.name: Papulopustular acne
variants.t: Inflamed papules and pustules with comedones; the commonest pattern.

variants.name: Truncal acne
variants.t: Papules, pustules and nodules across the back and chest.

variants.name: Nodulocystic acne
variants.t: Deep nodules and cysts with scarring. Refer for isotretinoin.

variants.name: Acne conglobata
variants.t: Interconnecting nodules, abscesses and sinus tracts on the trunk, with severe scarring.

variants.name: Acne fulminans
variants.t: Sudden painful **ulcerating, haemorrhagic** nodules with fever, malaise and joint pain, typically in young males; can follow starting isotretinoin. **Same-day** dermatology.

variants.name: SAPHO-associated acne
variants.t: Synovitis, acne, pustulosis, hyperostosis, osteitis: severe acne with bone or joint pain.

variants.name: Adult female acne
variants.t: Inflamed papules on the lower face and jawline; ask about the menstrual cycle and PCOS.

variants.name: Neonatal and infantile acne
variants.t: A separate pattern in babies; see the dedicated page.

sub: Redness is less visible; **post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation** is often the main reason to seek help and can last months.
Pomade acne is more common; **keloid scars** are more likely on the jawline, chest and upper back.
Treat inflammation early; azelaic acid helps pigmentation.
Topical and oral **retinoids** and **tetracyclines** are contraindicated.
**Benzoyl peroxide** with or without clindamycin can be used cautiously.
Look for irregular periods, **hirsutism**, acanthosis nigricans and weight gain.
Acne before age 8–9 is unusual: consider an endocrine cause and seek advice.

figs.caption: Skin of colour: post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation after truncal acne.
Acne with PCOS: check for hirsutism, irregular periods and acanthosis nigricans.
Acne in pregnancy: avoid retinoids and tetracyclines.

sections.title: Diagnosis and investigations
blocks: Diagnosis is **clinical**, from the lesion mix and distribution. **Comedones** are the key sign.

ul: Duration and course; **previous treatments**, how long each was used and adherence.
**Contraception and pregnancy plans**; current drugs (steroids, lithium, anabolic steroids, EGFR inhibitors).
**PCOS features**: irregular periods, hirsutism, weight gain.
Cosmetics, hair products and occlusion; picking.
**Psychosocial impact**, mood and any self-harm thoughts; scarring.
Lesion types and approximate counts; **nodules**; trunk involvement.
**Scarring** and pigment change.
Signs of hyperandrogenism (hirsutism, acanthosis nigricans, androgenic alopecia).

head: Category
Definition
rows: Any of: comedones; up to 34 inflammatory lesions; up to 2 nodules
35 or more inflammatory lesions, and/or 3 or more nodules
table.caption: NG198 uses this two-level split to choose a regimen.

figs.caption: Moderate: papules and pustules on the chin with early marks.
Severe: many papulopustules with early scarring.

ul: Other grading tools (Leeds, Investigator's Global Assessment, lesion counts) are mainly for specialist documentation and trials.
Record scarring, pigment change and psychological impact separately: they can justify referral at **any** severity.
**Usually none.**
**Hormone profile** (e.g. testosterone, SHBG, LH/FSH) if the picture is atypical or suggests hyperandrogenism or PCOS.
**Skin swab** if an unusual pustular infection is suspected (e.g. Gram-negative folliculitis after long antibiotic use).
Baseline bloods for isotretinoin are arranged by the specialist team.

ddx.name: Rosacea
ddx.f: Central facial flushing and telangiectasia; papules and pustules but **no comedones**; usually older adults; eye symptoms.

ddx.name: Perioral (periorificial) dermatitis
ddx.f: Small papules around the mouth, nose and eyes with a **spared rim** next to the lip; often triggered by topical steroid.

ddx.name: Bacterial folliculitis
ddx.f: Follicular pustules, often on the trunk, buttocks or beard area; **no comedones**; culture may help.

ddx.name: Malassezia (pityrosporum) folliculitis
ddx.f: Itchy, **monomorphic** papules and pustules on the upper trunk; worse with heat and antibiotics.

ddx.name: Milia
ddx.f: Tiny white keratin cysts; firm, not inflamed.

ddx.name: Acneiform drug eruption
ddx.f: Sudden, monomorphic eruption after starting a drug (steroids, EGFR inhibitors); no comedones.

ddx.name: Hidradenitis suppurativa
ddx.f: Recurrent nodules, abscesses and **tunnels in the flexures** (axillae, groin); double-ended comedones.

sections.title: Management

ul: Follow **NICE NG198**: agree one **12-week** course after shared decision-making (severity, preference, adverse effects, pregnancy plans).
Treat early to **prevent scarring**; set expectations that improvement takes **6–8 weeks** and full effect up to 12.
**Antimicrobial stewardship**: never use an antibiotic alone; always pair it with BPO or a topical retinoid.
Review at **12 weeks**; then step down to **maintenance**.
Ask about mood and offer support at every review.

blocks: Use the NG198 split above (**mild to moderate** vs **moderate to severe**) to choose a regimen. Scarring, pigment change or distress can justify escalation or referral at any severity.

ul: Wash **twice daily** with a syndet (non-alkaline) cleanser; avoid harsh scrubbing and over-cleansing.
Use **non-comedogenic** moisturisers, sunscreen and make-up; remove make-up at night.
**Do not pick or squeeze**: it causes scarring.
OTC **benzoyl peroxide** (or adapalene where available) while waiting for a prescription.
No specific diet is recommended (NICE).

drugs.name: Adapalene + benzoyl peroxide
drugs.dose: Once daily in the evening, 12 weeks.
drugs.use: First line at **any severity**; also maintenance.
drugs.cautions: Retinoid: **avoid in pregnancy** and when planning pregnancy. Irritation, dryness.
drugs.counsel: Start on alternate nights or as short contact; pea-sized amount to the whole area, not spot-treating. BPO **bleaches** fabric and hair. Use sunscreen.

drugs.name: Tretinoin + clindamycin
drugs.dose: Once daily in the evening, 12 weeks.
drugs.cautions: Retinoid: avoid in pregnancy. Contains an antibiotic: **do not combine with an oral antibiotic**.
drugs.counsel: Irritation and photosensitivity: start gradually and use sunscreen.

drugs.name: Benzoyl peroxide + clindamycin
drugs.cautions: Contains an antibiotic: not with oral antibiotics; can be used cautiously in pregnancy.

drugs.name: Benzoyl peroxide alone
drugs.use: If the patient wants to avoid a retinoid or antibiotic; OTC while awaiting review; maintenance.
drugs.cautions: Irritation; **bleaching** of towels, pillowcases and hair.
drugs.counsel: No bacterial resistance develops, so it is the preferred antibiotic partner.

drugs.name: Azelaic acid 15–20%
drugs.use: With an oral tetracycline for moderate to severe acne; alone for maintenance; helpful for **post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation**.

drugs.name: Lymecycline 408 mg
drugs.use: **Moderate to severe** acne, always **with** adapalene + BPO or azelaic acid.
drugs.cautions: **Contraindicated in pregnancy**, breastfeeding and under 12s. Never with a topical antibiotic.
drugs.counsel: Separate from antacids, iron, zinc and calcium. Photosensitivity: use sunscreen.

drugs.name: Doxycycline 100 mg
drugs.cautions: Contraindicated in pregnancy and under 12s. **Photosensitivity** is more marked.
drugs.counsel: Swallow with plenty of water, sitting or standing upright (oesophageal irritation). Separate from antacids, iron and calcium.

drugs.name: Trimethoprim or an oral macrolide
drugs.use: Only when tetracyclines are unsuitable, in the combinations set out in NG198.

drugs.name: Oral isotretinoin
drugs.use: Severe, scarring or treatment-resistant acne. Initiated **only by or under a consultant dermatologist-led team**; two independent prescribers must agree in **under-18s**.
cautions: **Highly teratogenic**: Pregnancy Prevention Programme for anyone who could become pregnant (highly effective contraception from 1 month before to 1 month after; supervised pregnancy test before, **monthly** during and 1 month after; **30-day** prescription limit, dispensed within **7 days**).
**No tetracyclines** (benign intracranial hypertension); no vitamin A supplements; a progestogen-only pill alone is not adequate contraception for the PPP.
Acne may flare in the first weeks; a severe flare can be isotretinoin-triggered acne fulminans.
counsel: **Mental health**: report low mood or suicidal thoughts; structured assessment at baseline and every visit.
**Sexual function**: possible erectile or libido problems, rarely persistent.
Dry lips and skin (lip balm), nosebleeds, muscle aches, photosensitivity.
drugs.monitor: LFTs and fasting lipids at baseline and about 1 month. Pharmacy checks the PPP before every supply.

figs.caption: Isotretinoin cheilitis: near-universal lip dryness; counsel regular lip balm.
Early flare on isotretinoin: warn patients; a severe flare needs urgent review.

ul: If hormonal contraception is wanted, a **combined oral contraceptive** can be added to topical treatment; it is preferred to a progestogen-only pill, which can worsen acne.
**Co-cyprindiol** (cyproterone acetate with ethinylestradiol) is an option in selected women (e.g. with PCOS) when other treatments fail. Discuss **VTE risk** and review at about 6 months.
**Spironolactone** is not among the NG198 options; dermatologists sometimes use it off-label for adult women.
Prescribing detail: [acne prescribing and the combined pill](condition:acne-prescribing-combined-pill).

ladder.t: Skin care, non-comedogenic products, no picking; OTC benzoyl peroxide.
12 weeks of **adapalene + BPO**, **tretinoin + clindamycin**, or **BPO + clindamycin**.
12 weeks of adapalene + BPO (or azelaic acid) **plus lymecycline 408 mg or doxycycline 100 mg** daily.
Once clear: adapalene + BPO, or adapalene, azelaic acid or BPO alone. Stop the oral antibiotic.
Isotretinoin, under MHRA measures and the Pregnancy Prevention Programme.

blocks.title: Antimicrobial stewardship
list: **Never** use a topical antibiotic alone, an oral antibiotic alone, or topical and oral antibiotics together.
Review at **12 weeks**. Stop the oral antibiotic once clear and continue the topical.
If improved but not clear, the oral antibiotic can continue for up to another 12 weeks. Use antibiotic regimens beyond 6 months only in exceptional cases, with 3-monthly review.

ul: Acne is linked with **depression, anxiety, low self-esteem** and, in adolescents, increased **suicidal ideation**, regardless of treatment.
Ask about mood at every visit, not only when isotretinoin is involved.
Significant distress or a mental health disorder is a reason to **refer at any severity**.
Signpost support (e.g. the British Skin Foundation, Changing Faces) and involve the GP or mental health services when needed.

refer.t: **Acne fulminans**: refer the same day to on-call dermatology.
Low mood, self-harm or suicidal thoughts: assess and escalate (mental health), especially around isotretinoin.
Diagnostic uncertainty; acne conglobata; nodulocystic acne.
Mild to moderate acne that has failed **two** completed courses; moderate to severe acne that has failed a regimen including an oral antibiotic.
**Scarring**, persistent pigment change, or psychological distress at **any** severity.

sections.title: Red flags and when to refer

refer.t: Sudden ulcerating, haemorrhagic nodules with **fever and joint pain** (acne fulminans), including after starting isotretinoin.
Suicidal thoughts or severe low mood.
Scarring or keloids starting at any severity; acne before age 8–9 or with virilisation (endocrine cause).
Sudden monomorphic eruption after a new drug: review the drug.

figs.caption: Acne fulminans with ulceration and crusting: same-day dermatology.

sections.title: Complications and prognosis

sub: Atrophic: **ice-pick**, rolling and boxcar scars.
Hypertrophic and **keloid** scars, especially on the jawline, chest and shoulders in skin of colour.

ul: **Post-inflammatory erythema** (red marks, fair skin) and **hyperpigmentation** (dark marks, skin of colour).
**Psychological**: depression, anxiety, social withdrawal.
Treatment-related: antibiotic resistance, irritant dermatitis, isotretinoin adverse effects.

figs.caption: Ice-pick atrophic scars: scarring is a referral trigger at any severity.
Post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation in skin of colour.
Keloid scars on the shoulders after acne.

blocks: Scar treatment (and the timing of procedures around isotretinoin) is covered on [acne scars](condition:acne-scars) and [keloids](condition:keloids-hypertrophic-scars).

ul: Most adolescent acne improves by the **early to mid-20s**, but it can persist or start in adulthood.
Relapse after stopping treatment is common: **maintenance** treatment reduces it.
Early effective treatment is the best way to prevent permanent scarring.

pearls: Start topicals on **alternate days** or as short-contact applications, then build up.
Apply topicals to the **whole affected area**, not just individual spots.
BPO **bleaches** fabric and hair: warn about towels and pillowcases.
Retinoids and tetracyclines cause **photosensitivity**: give sun advice.
**Pregnancy**: no topical or oral retinoids, no tetracyclines; BPO ± clindamycin can be used cautiously.
If hormonal contraception is wanted, a **combined pill** is preferred over a progestogen-only pill.
**Combination rules**: always pair an oral antibiotic with BPO and/or a topical retinoid; review at 12 weeks.
When referring for isotretinoin, document mental health history thoroughly.
In skin of colour, treat early and consider azelaic acid for pigmentation.
Depression is common with acne itself: screen regardless of the drug.
Related: [retinoids](condition:retinoids), [acne mimics](condition:acne-mimics), [acne prescribing and the combined pill](condition:acne-prescribing-combined-pill).

quiz.q: What is the hallmark lesion that separates acne from rosacea?
Name the four pathogenic factors in acne.
quiz.a: Androgen-driven sebum, follicular hyperkeratinisation, *C. acnes* proliferation and inflammation.

quiz.q: How does NICE NG198 define moderate to severe acne?
quiz.a: 35 or more inflammatory lesions and/or 3 or more nodules.

quiz.q: Which first-line option suits any severity?
quiz.a: Fixed adapalene + BPO, or fixed tretinoin + clindamycin, once daily in the evening for 12 weeks.

quiz.q: Name three antibiotic combinations to avoid.
quiz.a: Topical antibiotic alone; oral antibiotic alone; topical and oral antibiotics together.

quiz.q: Why must tetracyclines not be given with isotretinoin?
Which acne patient needs same-day referral?
quiz.a: Acne fulminans: systemically unwell with ulcerating nodules.

quiz.q: Is a specific acne diet recommended?
quiz.a: No: NICE finds insufficient evidence for any specific diet.
